title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
1 Introduction
A model edit that changes one behaviour usually changes others too. Model-editing work evaluates locality: inputs outside an edit’s scope should keep their predictions (Yao et al. 2023, sec. 2). ROME, for example, scores an edited fact by whether the model retains facts about nearby subjects (Meng et al. 2022, sec. 3.3).
I use deliberate language damage as a controlled test of edit selectivity: each edit is calibrated to the same target-language damage on validation text, then evaluated for its effects on another language. A demanding neighbour for a language edit is a closely related language. Zeroing the parameters or neurons most important for one language also degrades its relatives: Spanish removal raises Italian and Portuguese perplexity (Zhang et al. 2024, Table 11), and deactivating French neurons also affects Spanish (Tang et al. 2024, sec. 3.3.1).
Parameter decompositions may allow narrower edits. adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD)1 approximates each weight matrix of a model by a sum of rank-one subcomponents, trained so that few are needed on any input (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2). It follows earlier attribution-based and stochastic decompositions (Braun et al. 2025; Bushnaq et al. 2025). If a subcomponent is specific to one language, an edit along it, \(W \leftarrow W + \alpha A\), might change that language and spare its relatives. This study uses Goodfire’s four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model decomposed in the VPD report.
This study is a small follow-up inspired by Lucius Bushnaq’s LessWrong post, “Exploration: fine-tuning with parameter decomposition”. Bushnaq trains the scalar prefactors of selected subcomponents of the same model to suppress German. One subcomponent, chosen by its interpretation label, reaches chance-level German with little English damage and spares French and Spanish, while also damaging Italian (Bushnaq 2026). His comparison uses matched training budgets and LoRA baselines, with varying achieved effects.
I extend Bushnaq’s scalar-edit comparison to three language pairs with a fixed rule for selecting one subcomponent per target from target and English text. I match target effects on validation text and add full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron baselines.
The pairs are German (de) and Dutch (nl), Spanish (es) and Portuguese (pt), and French (fr) and Italian (it). In each pair the related language is protected: it is evaluated after selection and training. I calibrate each edit to raise target cross-entropy (CE) by τ = 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text.
The outcome is the CE rise of the protected language on European Parliament session text (Koehn 2005). After fixing the six edits and comparators, I evaluate them once on 58 new session dates to test whether the difference in related-language damage carries over to new text.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
2 Setup
The method details give data sizes, selection and training recipes, and interval construction.
Model and subcomponents. The base model \(W_0\) is the four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model decomposed in the VPD report. It was trained on a subset of the Pile (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Edits act on its 24 weight matrices: in each layer, the query, key, value and output projections of attention and the two MLP matrices. The decomposition supplies 38,912 rank-one subcomponents in all, each of the form \(A_c = u_c v_c^\top\). Subcomponents are named by layer, matrix and index: 0.attn.o:268 is subcomponent 268 of the attention output projection of layer 0.
The edit. An edit along subcomponent \(c\) of matrix \(m\) is \(W_m \leftarrow W_m + \alpha A_c\), with the subcomponent not normalized. In VPD every subcomponent carries a mask coefficient that equals 1 in the unedited model. The edit moves it to \(1 + \alpha\). We write \(\alpha = s \cdot a\), with a sign \(s = \pm 1\) and a dose \(a > 0\). With \(s = -1\), as for every subcomponent selected here, the coefficient is \(1 - a\): a dose below 1 shrinks the subcomponent’s contribution, a dose of 1 removes it, and a dose above 1 reverses its sign. All other subcomponents and the decomposition residual stay fixed. The edit norm is \(|\alpha|\,\lVert A_c\rVert_F\).
Text and effects. Every Europarl set has one window per session date, parallel across languages. The CE rise of an edit is measured in nat/token. For each window, I subtract the base model \(W_0\)’s mean next-token CE from the edited model’s, then average these differences over windows. Each target has three overlapping draws of its Europarl training windows. The English retain pool mixes Europarl English training text, WikiText-2 validation text (Merity et al. 2017) and English-filtered Pile validation text.

2.1 Selecting the subcomponent
The rule scores each subcomponent by its local effect on target CE relative to its local effect on English output. Let \(g_c\) be the derivative of the mean target CE on the draw with respect to the subcomponent’s mask coefficient. Let \(q_c\) be the curvature of the English output along the same coordinate, estimated on the retain pool with labels sampled from \(W_0\). This estimates the directional Fisher information of the model’s predictive distribution. The rule ranks subcomponents by the gradient-to-retain-curvature score \[\frac{g_c^2}{q_c + \varepsilon \lVert A_c\rVert^2},\] where a small floor \(\varepsilon\) keeps subcomponents with almost no measured curvature from dominating.
The rule then tests a shortlist of the best-ranked subcomponents on the target training draw. For each subcomponent, with sign \(s = \operatorname{sign}(g_c)\), it raises the dose step by step up to 2. It accepts the first subcomponent whose target CE rise reaches 1 nat/token. If none does, it accepts the first that reached 0.5, and otherwise it finds no feasible subcomponent.
The rule chose the same subcomponent in all three draws of each target: 0.attn.o:268 for German, 0.attn.o:676 for Spanish and 0.attn.o:640 for French. They all lie in the attention output projection of the first layer and have sign \(-1\).


2.2 Comparators
The comparators test other ways to produce the target effect, with different choices of which weights may change. Like the selection rule, they use only target and English text for selection and training.

Rank-one LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) learns both update vectors in layer 0’s attention output matrix, matching the subcomponent edit’s matrix and rank while learning its own direction.
Full-matrix fine-tuning updates all 24 weight matrices, allowing a broader learned edit.
Neuron edits use the top \(k\) MLP neurons ranked by how much more often they are active on the target draw than on the English retain pool. The edit scales their output weights down, with \(k\) and the scale calibrated to τ, in the spirit of language-specific neurons (Tang et al. 2024; Kojima et al. 2024). This localizes the edit through neuron activity rather than a decomposition of the weights.
The randomized-dictionary control applies the same selection rule to a randomized dictionary. In each matrix, one random signed permutation transforms the output coordinates of every subcomponent, and another transforms the input coordinates. This preserves their norms and pairwise angles but removes their alignment with \(W_0\).

The two learned updates are trained separately for each draw, for 200 steps. They minimize a per-window hinge penalty for target CE rises below 1 nat/token, plus the KL divergence from \(W_0\) on the English retain pool with weight 1. The final update is scaled down to reach τ.
Additional comparisons vary the choice of a single subcomponent within the same dictionary. They use a separate multiplicity correction and receive no confirmatory verdicts (Section 3.6).


2.3 Calibration and the six edits
An edit could spare the protected language simply because it has little effect on the target. To compare methods at a common target effect, I calibrate every method on target Europarl validation text. A short search over its dose sets the target CE rise to τ. An edit is matched if its validation effect lies within 0.02 nat/token of τ. Only matched edits enter a contrast. The effects achieved on the readout dates can differ and are reported with the results.

2.4 What was fixed, and what was known
Selection and training used only target and English text. Earlier research had used protected-language development text and identified the German subcomponent, so the selection history was not blind (Section 7.3).
I fixed the edits, comparators and analysis before evaluating them once on 58 further session dates. Those dates were not used for selection, calibration or re-matching. This tests the six fixed edits on new text in the same languages. Evaluating the selection procedure itself remains an open question.


2.5 Readouts, eligibility and intervals
Guards. English test sets determine which matched edits are usable: Europarl, WikiText-2 and Pile test text on the development readout, and English text from the confirmatory dates on the confirmatory readout. An edit is unusable if any guard’s CE rises by more than 0.1 nat/token. On the confirmatory dates it must also have been usable on development. This is an eligibility rule fixed in advance. Two usable edits can still differ greatly in how much they change English (Section 3.4).
Contrasts. For each protected-language session date, a contrast takes the CE rise of the subcomponent edit minus that of the comparator, averaged over the draws in which both are matched and usable. Its estimate is the mean over dates. Negative values mean less protected-language damage for the subcomponent edit. The claim family comprises four comparators × three pairs × two values of τ, or 24 planned contrasts.
Intervals. Every confidence interval in this paper is a simultaneous 95% interval from a bootstrap over session dates (Efron 1979), with one resample shared by every contrast of a family and the max-|t| critical value of a simultaneous band (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller 2019, supplement, Algorithm 3). The intervals describe uncertainty across session dates for these fixed edits. The bootstrap varies dates while holding the draws, training seeds, subcomponents, language pairs and model fixed.
Confirmatory verdicts. Each claim contrast with a development interval receives one verdict on the confirmatory readout, according to a rule table fixed before the set was opened. It is “reproduced on confirm” if its interval excludes zero with the development sign and no used draw has a target CE rise outside τ ± 0.1. A rise outside this band is the target flag.
Post hoc analyses. Two analyses were chosen after the results were known, outside the protocol. The frozen verdicts remain those of the original analysis. The first asks whether the target effects achieved on the readout dates were comparable (Section 3.3). The second counts how often the learned updates move English less (Section 3.4).

3 Results

3.1 Target change against protected damage
Figure 1 places the intended target effect next to the unwanted protected-language damage. All matched edits passed the English guards, and on the confirmatory dates no edit raised the target flag. At both values of τ and for all three pairs, the subcomponent edits have the lowest protected-language CE rise. Across the six subcomponent edits, the protected-language rise is 0.0003 to 0.0053 nat/token. The other methods raise it by about 0.03 to 0.88 (Table 2).






Figure 1: Target CE rise against protected CE rise for every edit on the 58 confirmatory dates (subcomponent edits: one per pair and τ, other methods: one per draw). The bands mark τ ± 0.1, the frozen tolerance of the target flag.





3.2 The protected contrasts
To assess the protected-language differences across session dates, I compare each subcomponent edit directly with each comparator. On the confirmatory dates, all 18 claim contrasts that have an estimate lie below zero, with upper interval ends at −0.023 or below, and every verdict is “reproduced on confirm” (Figure 2, top row, Table 3). The largest difference between a confirmatory estimate and its development estimate is 0.033.
The 18 contrasts share six subcomponent edits: each edit is compared with three comparators. Across draws, the comparators’ training samples and the learned updates’ random seeds vary; the subcomponent edits stay fixed. The contrasts are therefore dependent.


3.3 Achieved target effects
The edits were calibrated to the same effect on validation text. On the readout dates the achieved effects differ somewhat (Figure 1). To assess whether less protected damage came with a smaller target effect, I estimated, post hoc, the difference in target CE rise between the subcomponent edit and each comparator, its target gap, in one simultaneous family with the protected contrasts (method details). A target gap counts as agreement if its whole interval lies within ±0.1 nat/token. This band was chosen after the results. It compares two methods and is separate from the frozen target flag, which compares one edit with τ.






Figure 2: Contrasts of the subcomponent edit with each claim comparator, on the confirmatory (filled, upper marker) and development (open, lower marker) dates, with simultaneous 95% intervals. Top: difference in protected CE rise, the frozen claim family. The axes differ between columns. Bottom: difference in achieved target CE rise, from the post hoc family of Section 3.3, with the ±0.1 nat/token agreement band. Negative values in the top row mean less protected-language damage for the subcomponent edit. Positive values in the bottom row mean a larger target effect.



On the confirmatory dates, 15 of the 18 target gaps agree by this criterion (Figure 2, bottom row). The three exceptions are all at τ = 1, and in each the point estimate lies inside the band:

German and Dutch against rank-one LoRA: +0.057 [+0.007, +0.107]
French and Italian against full-matrix fine-tuning: +0.077 [+0.020, +0.134]
French and Italian against rank-one LoRA: +0.038 [−0.027, +0.104].

On the development dates, 17 of 18 target gaps agree. The exception is French and Italian against full-matrix fine-tuning. All four exceptions have positive point estimates, though the interval for French and Italian against rank-one LoRA permits a smaller target effect for the subcomponent edit. In this larger post hoc family, all 18 protected-CE intervals and all 18 protected-KL intervals lie below zero on both readouts. Protected KL is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0} \,\|\, p_{\text{edit}})\), averaged over next-token positions on protected-language text.


3.4 English: where the learned updates are better
Less damage to the related language does not imply better preservation of English. The guard rule only asks whether English CE rose past its limit. A finer measure is the KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0} \,\|\, p_{\text{edit}})\) of the edited model’s English next-token distribution from that of \(W_0\), averaged over positions. By this measure, both learned updates preserve English better than the subcomponent edits (Table 2). On the development readout, over three pairs × three draws × two values of τ × four English sets (the validation set and the three guards), the LoRA update has the lower KL in 72 of 72 comparisons and full-matrix fine-tuning in 65 of 72. On the English confirmatory text both have the lower KL in 18 of 18.
The subcomponent edits also change English little in absolute terms: their English KL on the confirmatory dates is below 10⁻³ nat/token. Their weight changes have larger norms: 0.29 to 0.47, against 0.12 to 0.24 for the LoRA updates and 0.07 to 0.11 for full-matrix fine-tuning. The learned updates were trained with an explicit English KL term. None of the methods had a term for the protected language. The comparison therefore measures how well the methods spare a related language absent from their training objective.

3.5 The randomized-dictionary control gave no estimate
The randomized-dictionary control was intended to test how selective an edit of the same form is when the subcomponents are unrelated to the model’s weights. Applying the same selection rule, it found no feasible subcomponent in any of the 9 target–draw combinations: no shortlisted subcomponent reached even 0.5 nat/token on the target training draw within the dose limit of 2. The randomized-dictionary control therefore has no edit, and its six claim contrasts have no estimate. Because some planned contrasts are empty, the frozen analysis has the overall status “conditional” rather than “complete”.
No comparison was possible within the dose limit. Larger doses remain untested, and the alternative selectors do not isolate the dictionary’s contribution either (Section 3.6; Section 4).


3.6 Subcomponents chosen by other rules
Four alternatives test other choices within the same dictionary. Two take the first step of orthogonal matching pursuit (Pati et al. 1993; Mallat and Zhang 1993): the subcomponent with the largest absolute correlation with a learned update, using that correlation’s sign. One uses the full-matrix fine-tuning update; the other uses a rank-one LoRA across all 24 matrices, unlike the main one-matrix LoRA comparator. A causal-importance heuristic chooses the largest mean target-minus-English importance and a negative sign, using the per-position importance learned in VPD (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2.3). It adapts Bushnaq’s top-16 ranking to one subcomponent (Bushnaq 2026). The fourth reuses the previously chosen German subcomponent.
All alternatives use the same calibration rule. Some failed to reach τ or lacked an eligible learned-update checkpoint, so some contrasts use fewer draws and others have no estimate. Every estimable contrast is at or below zero. The causal-importance heuristic picked 0.attn.o:41 in 8 of 9 target–draw combinations and, on the confirmatory dates, raised protected CE by 0.48 to 1.37 nat/token more than the selected subcomponent, at achieved target rises close to the selected subcomponent’s. The previously chosen German subcomponent gives an identical edit. Selectivity therefore varies among subcomponents of the same dictionary.

section: 4 Longer training and alternative rank-one directions
text:
4 Longer training and alternative rank-one directions
The main comparison leaves open how the result depends on the learned updates’ training recipe and on the available rank-one directions. After the confirmatory readout, I examined these dependencies in exploratory comparisons on the previously evaluated development dates. The six subcomponent edits were compared with learned updates trained for 2,000 steps and a whitened selector that searches rank-one directions outside the VPD dictionary using the target gradient and an approximate English Fisher curvature. All were calibrated to the same τ. A separate SVD control applies the selection rule to singular components of the original weight matrices. All 18 protected-CE intervals of the all-run family and all 12 of the family excluding unstable learned runs lie below zero. The achieved target rises differ by at most 0.07 nat/token. The appendix gives the comparison rules and chronology.
The expanded training recipe lowered the protected-language rise of full-matrix fine-tuning in all six target and τ combinations and that of LoRA in five of six. Steps, margin, grid and seeds changed together, with retention still limited to English. Convergence remains unestablished at either budget.
The whitened rank-one selector uses the selected VPD subcomponent’s norm and the main selector’s ε, leaving the dictionary’s contribution entangled with the selector’s. The SVD comparator gave no estimate: every edit that reached τ raised an English guard by more than 0.1 nat/token, and three of nine did not reach τ = 1.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
5 Limits of these conclusions
The result covers six edits in one four-layer model, three language pairs and two values of τ. The measured outcomes are protected-language CE on parliamentary text and English CE guards and KL. The confirmatory readout tests fixed edits on new text in the same languages; uncertainty varies session dates only (Section 2.5). Calibration matches mean target effects, while the learned updates optimize a per-window hinge. English retention is not matched across methods. Testing the selection rule in other models, explaining the edits’ selectivity and evaluating tasks beyond next-token prediction remain open.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
6 Conclusion
Across three language pairs in this model, six subcomponent edits raised related-language CE by at most 0.0053 nat/token on 58 new session dates. All 18 simultaneous 95% intervals for the differences from the three comparators lie below zero. Target effects were matched at 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text; in a post hoc check on evaluation text, 15 of the 18 target-gap intervals lay wholly within ±0.1 nat/token. The three remaining mean gaps were positive, though one interval also allowed a smaller subcomponent effect. Learned updates preserved English output better.
Exploratory comparisons on previously evaluated development dates also favoured subcomponent edits for related-language damage against a whitened rank-one selector and learned updates trained for 2,000 steps. These results concern fixed edits: prior protected-language access (Section 2.4) and the inconclusive randomized-dictionary control leave the selection rule’s generalization and the dictionary’s contribution unresolved.
AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for research planning, code development, data analysis, and manuscript preparation. Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

text:
7 Method details

Text. Europarl v7 (Koehn 2005) supplies one 257-token window per session date (256 predictions). Each target has three draws of 64 of its 128 training windows and 32 validation windows for calibration. The English validation set has 64 windows: 32 Europarl and 32 English-filtered Pile. The retain pool has 256 windows: 128 Europarl English training, 64 WikiText-2 validation and 64 English-filtered Pile validation.
Selection. For softmax cross-entropy, the model Fisher equals the generalized Gauss–Newton matrix (Martens 2020, sec. 9.2), unlike the empirical Fisher based on data labels (Kunstner et al. 2019, sec. 1). The estimate \(q_c\) averages squared directional scores using eight model-sampled label sets per retain window. The floor \(\varepsilon\) is the 1st percentile of \(q_c / \lVert A_c\rVert^2\). The top 64 subcomponents are re-ranked using the larger of \(q_c\) and a second estimate on 256 other English windows, before the dose search of Section 2.1. Curvature checks passed on the NVIDIA L40S used for the original runs, but the batch-splitting check failed on the tested A10 and L4. Verified selector reruns cover only the German target’s first draw on the L40S, with the VPD dictionary and one randomized dictionary. GPU-dependent Fisher-label sampling can change selections on other hardware.
Calibration. The first dose-grid crossing of τ is bracketed, then bisected for at most five steps until within the matching tolerance. Neuron edits scale the top \(k\) neurons’ output weights by \(1-f\): calibration takes the smallest power-of-two \(k\) from 1 to 256 whose full removal reaches τ, then calibrates \(f\). Randomized dictionaries use a separate seed per draw.
Learned updates. The 200-step updates use Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015), 10 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 8 target and 8 English windows per step. Calibration scales the final update \(D\) to \(\beta D\), with \(\beta \le 1\). The learning rate is chosen once per target on draw 0, by the lowest English validation KL at τ = 1. Every target chose 3e-3 for LoRA and 1e-6 for full-matrix fine-tuning, respectively the upper and lower edges of the tested grids.

7.1 Extended comparisons
The extended learned updates use 2,000 steps, a hinge margin of 1.5, wider learning-rate grids and three seeds per draw. The whitened selector maximizes the squared target gradient relative to damped K-FAC curvature on English text (Martens and Grosse 2015), then tests doses from 1/64 to 8. The SVD control applies the main selection rule unchanged to the singular components of all 24 weight matrices; these reconstruct the weights exactly, whereas VPD leaves a residual. The exploratory rerun selected the same VPD subcomponents in all nine target–draw combinations.
Contrasts compare unpaired means over each method’s matched and usable runs in one simultaneous family. A second family excludes unstable learned runs: 7 of 27 LoRA runs had English validation KL at step 2,000 greater than twice their minimum from step 100 onward. Training diagnostics did not establish objective convergence and were not used to select edits.
The comparisons were specified before the runs, on 12 October 2026. A 5% tolerance for reproducing the curvature floor across GPU models was added after one selection finished, before its result was read. Analysis rules were fixed before readout, after selection outcomes, learning-rate choices and the rate grid’s target and English validation effects were known. The analyzer’s interval checks were implemented after readout but before its measurements were opened or analysed. This chronology comes from the author’s records and is not independently timestamped.


7.2 Readouts and intervals
Readouts. Development guards use Europarl English test text (64 windows), WikiText-2 test text (32) and Pile test documents (512). The confirmatory guard uses English from the 58 confirmatory dates, comprising 48 main and 10 reserve dates analysed together.
Intervals. The bootstrap uses 2,000 date resamples with replacement, shared across each family. A contrast’s standard error is the standard deviation of its resampled means. Its interval is the estimate ± \(c\) standard errors, where \(c\) is the 95% quantile of the largest absolute standardized deviation in the family.
Verdicts. The first applicable rule determines the result: missing intervals or technical failures give “not established”; a target flag in any used draw gives “effect not maintained”; an interval excluding zero with the development sign gives “reproduced on confirm”, or with the opposite sign “not reproduced”. All other cases are “not established”.
Target gaps. The post hoc family has 54 coordinates per readout: target gaps, protected-CE contrasts and protected-KL contrasts. Per-date values are averaged over draws, with 20,000 shared date resamples.


7.3 Protocol records and prior access

Freeze and readout. The selection, comparison and analysis rules were frozen on 11 October 2026, immediately before the development readout. Later that day, the unchanged edits were evaluated once on 58 further dates, under an amendment fixed before any of those windows was parsed.
Prior knowledge. German subcomponent 0.attn.o:268 had been chosen with Dutch in view in an earlier experiment and was the top German candidate in a pilot of this selector. Dutch, Portuguese and Italian development text and NTREX Dutch and Italian text (Federmann et al. 2022) had been read or used previously. The 64 development dates therefore do not provide a fresh test.
Pretraining. The Pile contains a European Parliament component (Gao et al. 2020, sec. 2.17); whether the model’s training subset includes it is unknown. Dates new to this workflow may have appeared in pretraining.
Record limits. The chronology relies on the author’s documents and run log, without independent timestamps. The original protocol, freeze record and frozen code list are unpublished. Their hashes identify contents but do not establish dates, so there is no timestamped preregistration.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
1 Introduction
Repeating a fine-tuning recipe on new samples can reproduce its collateral damage, so a repair learned for an earlier fine-tune may help repair the next one. The earlier fine-tune is the donor and its repair is the donor repair. We can keep the donor repair’s directions fixed and fit new scalar coefficients, or use it to initialize a repair whose directions can change.
The fine-tuning procedure deliberately worsens German next-token prediction and, as a side effect, raises Dutch cross-entropy (CE), a measure of prediction loss. This provides a controlled test: the repair must restore Dutch prediction quality while preserving the intended German change. I train the donor and two target fine-tunes independently from the same base model, using the same recipe on different samples from the same Europarl data distribution. The donor repair has one rank-one update per weight matrix. The primary comparison asks how much Dutch damage is recovered by rescaling its fixed directions and by allowing those directions to change. The descriptive secondary comparisons ask how donor initialization performs against fresh and random starts at each fit budget and step cap, and what it saves (Table 1).
I fit rank-one repairs with a KL objective on the model used in Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) study (Bushnaq et al. 2026). The repairs operate directly on its weight matrices, independently of the decomposition.
Several methods reuse a weight update with fixed or learned scales. Task arithmetic adds or subtracts a weight difference with a single scale (Ilharco et al. 2023). RESTA adds one separately obtained safety vector to fine-tunes in several domains, using a fixed global scale in its main experiments (Bhardwaj et al. 2024). SafeGene keeps a distilled safety adapter frozen and learns one scalar per selected layer, improving on a coefficient of 1 (Wang et al. 2026, sec. 3.5 and 4.4). Such reuse can also fail. EnchTable’s preprint Table II reports a medical fine-tune that RESTA leaves less safe than before (Wu et al. 2026). Other work uses a learned object to initialize new training. In SPoT, soft prompts learned on source tasks initialize the prompt of a target task (Vu et al. 2022). These studies do not compare the two uses of one transferred update on the same target at matched rank and cost. This study makes that comparison at matched rank and reports the costs of each family.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
2 Setup
Model and fine-tunes. The base model is Goodfire’s four-layer decoder-only model of 67M parameters, trained on a subset of the Pile (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Each fine-tune trains an additive update \(D\) to the 24 weight matrices of the attention and MLP blocks. Embeddings and norms stay frozen. A hinge term raises German CE, and a KL term keeps English, French, Spanish and Italian, the retain languages, close to the base model. The text is Europarl session text (Koehn 2005). The donor fine-tune and the two targets follow the same recipe with different seeds and training dates (method details). Dutch is held out of fine-tuning. On the readout dates the primary target’s Dutch damage is 0.187 nat/token [0.178, 0.196] and the replication target’s 0.189 [0.180, 0.198].
Repair. A repair adds \(E_m = b_m a_m^{\top}\) to each of the 24 matrices of the fine-tuned model, so it has rank one per matrix. The vector \(a_m\) is the input factor and \(b_m\) is the output factor. The repair minimizes KL divergence from two teacher models across three groups of text. The fine-tuned model is the teacher on German, to preserve the intended effect, and on the retain languages. The base model is the teacher on Dutch, to undo the damage. Each term uses \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{teacher}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\), averaged over the group’s predicted positions. The loss sums the mean KL of the three groups with equal weights. The repair norm is capped at the fine-tune norm, \(\lVert E\rVert_F \le \lVert D\rVert_F\). Every target-repair family trains full-batch for 600 steps at four learning rates and keeps checkpoints as candidates for selection. Families initialized from the donor repair scale it down if needed to meet the norm cap (method details).
I first learned the donor repair from a fresh rank-one initialization (zero output vectors, random input vectors) on 73,728 prediction positions, using three learning rates and 200 minibatch steps per run. The same selected donor repair is reused for both targets.
Recovery. Recovery is the share of the fine-tune’s Dutch damage that a repair \(X\) removes, \[r_{\text{nl}}(X) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(X) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{fine-tuned}) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}.\] Differences in recovery are reported in percentage points (pp).
In the scalar-only family, each donor repair update stays fixed and the repair is \(E_m = c_m b_m a_m^{\top}\). Fitting the coefficients \(c_m\) trains 24 parameters. The other families train one or both factors, as listed in Table 1.

Varying the fit budget and the step cap tests whether donor initialization helps chiefly when fitting data and training steps are limited. Fresh fitting uses LoRA’s zero-output initialization (Hu et al. 2022). Unlike the random frozen input vectors studied by Zhu et al. (2024), output-only fitting here freezes the donor repair’s trained input vectors. A second seed of fresh and of random initialization, at the full budget only, shows how far a result moves between initializations. The first fresh seed starts from the same input vectors used to initialize the donor repair, while the second uses an independent draw.
Budgets and step caps. Each target has nested fit budgets of 256, 512 and 2,048 unique predicted tokens with a 2:1:1 split of Dutch, German and retain text. These budgets count prediction positions, excluding the initial context token of each window. A separate selection and diagnostic pool contains 57,344 prediction positions, shared by all families. The targets share repair-fitting, selection and readout windows; their fine-tuning seeds and training windows differ. Checkpoints at steps ≤50, ≤100 and ≤200 of the same runs form step-capped cells, alongside the full 600-step runs. Each family therefore has a grid of 3 budgets × 4 step caps. The cost appendix gives the costs of selection and of the additional scalar optimization.
Selection and readout. For every family and cell, a fixed rule chooses one candidate on separate selection dates: among the candidates that keep the fine-tune’s German effect and move Dutch toward the base model, it prefers higher Dutch recovery, subject to a guard against raising the CE of the retain languages (method details). The chosen repairs are read out once on 92 session dates from the validation period, separate from the project’s earlier data windows (data details). The selected checkpoint can precede the cell’s step cap. All cells of a target share one bootstrap over readout dates (Efron 1979), so contrasts are paired. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals.
Additional scalar optimization. A scalar-only shortfall could reflect unfinished optimization. To check this, at the 2,048-token budget, two additional projected-gradient runs optimize the same full-batch fit loss from two starts, using the convergence criteria in the appendix. The label “+ full-batch optimization” refers to these extra runs; ordinary fitting also uses full batches. Selection includes the 48 training checkpoints and the 2 converged candidates, so an ordinary checkpoint can still supply the reported result (appendix).
Interpretation rules. The primary contrast compares donor initialization with the scalar-only search with full-batch optimization at 2,048 tokens and 600 steps. An advantage of more than 3 pp is established if its whole interval lies above 3 pp, excluded if the whole interval lies below 3 pp, and undecided otherwise. I interpret this contrast on a target only if its Dutch damage is clear (the lower end of the readout interval is at least 0.025 nat/token), both selected repairs satisfy the readout constraints in Table 6, and scalar optimization converged from both starts. All other contrasts are descriptive, without multiplicity correction. Their intervals determine whether the sign is positive, negative or undecided. Five contrasts, marked in Table 3, are also assessed for equivalence within a ±2 pp band. The protocol fixes both margins without a stated derivation.

3 Results

3.1 Fixed directions fall short
Both targets meet the conditions for interpreting the primary contrast (Table 6 and Table 7). Donor initialization recovers 11.3 pp [+10.0, +12.7] more damage than the scalar-only search with full-batch optimization on the primary target (Table 2) and 20.4 pp [+19.0, +21.7] more on the replication target. Both intervals lie entirely above the 3 pp margin.
The gap is nearly as large at 256 and 512 tokens, where scalar fitting received no additional optimization to convergence (Figure 1). Scalar-only fitting recovers about 87% of the damage on the primary target and 77% on the replication target, and adding the converged candidates changes this little (Table 3). Every family that trains the factors recovers at least 95.6%. A corresponding shortfall appears on the scalar-only repair’s own fit tokens, measured by recovery of Dutch KL divergence from the base model rather than CE recovery (appendix).
The output-only control tests how much of this gap can be closed while keeping the donor repair’s input vectors fixed. It closes most of the gap (Table 3); training both factors recovers only slightly more. Without an output-only control with frozen random input vectors, this result does not isolate the contribution of the donor repair’s learned input vectors (control details).

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
4 Limits of these conclusions
The experiment uses one donor, one recipe and one model, with each target analysed separately. The bootstrap quantifies variation across readout dates for those targets. Variation across fine-tunes, donors and recipes remains unmeasured. Second seeds were run at the full budget only, leaving short-run advantages unassessed against seed variation.
The scalar-only shortfall applies to the tested search and norm cap (optimization details). The mechanism and the contribution of the donor repair’s input vectors remain unresolved (control details). The cost projection uses the first fresh seed as its reference and depends on the chosen ±2 pp quality criterion and tested grid (cost accounting).
The repair addresses collateral Dutch CE damage after a fine-tune that deliberately worsens German prediction. Safety alignment and transfer of a new skill remain outside the study’s scope.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
5 Conclusion
For this model, donor and recipe, training the donor repair’s directions outperformed the tested scalar-only search, including its converged full-batch candidates. Donor initialization helped most with little fitting data and few steps. At the full budget, its advantage over fresh fitting was positive but within the ±2 pp equivalence band and comparable to fresh-seed differences. On the tested grid, its cheapest reaching cell used one eighth as many fit-token presentations as fresh fitting’s cheapest reaching cell, while both families reached the reference with 256 unique fit tokens.

Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

6 Method details

Fine-tunes. Each fine-tune learns full-matrix additive updates \(D_m\) to the query, key, value, output and two MLP matrices of each layer (24 matrices). Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) runs at learning rate 3e-6 for 200 steps on the per-window hinge \(\max(0, 1 - \Delta\mathrm{CE}_{\text{de}})\) (1-nat margin) plus retain-language KL with weight 1. The checkpoint is chosen on German validation dates.
Repairs. Ordinary donor and target fitting uses Adam. Donor checkpoints are saved every 25 steps and selected on the donor’s validation windows by the rule below. Target repairs save checkpoints every 50 steps at the four learning rates in Table 5, giving 48 candidates per family. Donor starts are capped as \(\min(1, \lVert D\rVert_F / \lVert E_{\text{donor}}\rVert_F)\, E_{\text{donor}}\); fresh initialization is defined in Table 1.

The same grid serves the 50-step cap. Several output-only cells and the donor-initialized replication cell at 512 tokens select the first checkpoint at the lowest rate; reuse alone can explain repeated values across caps. Selection. Feasibility requires a German-damage ratio (with repair / without repair) of 0.9–1.1, German KL drift from the fine-tuned model at most 0.05 times the base model’s KL from that fine-tune, and Dutch movement toward the base model. Feasible candidates are ranked by Dutch recovery, then smaller norm, then listing order. Among the top five, the first raising no retain language’s CE by more than 0.01 nat/token is chosen.
Data. Portuguese, the seventh language, is diagnostic only on selection and readout dates. Its selection windows count toward token and evaluation costs, but it enters neither the loss nor selection constraints.
A readout date was ineligible if found in recorded project data, pilot or run files, or if its window duplicated text already in use. All dates passed; prior model exposure remains unresolved. Selection and readout use 32 and 92 dates, respectively, each providing one 257-token window (256 predictions) from the same turn in every language. Target fit windows and selection dates are separate from the donor’s. The fit budgets are nested: at 256 tokens, one Dutch window contributes 128 predictions, one German 64, and four retain windows 16 each; 512 doubles these prediction counts. At 2,048 tokens, four Dutch and two German windows contribute 256 predictions each, and one window per retain language contributes 128.
Study record. According to my records, a dated protocol fixed rules, margins and families before readout-data construction and target fine-tuning. An author-dated amendment before any target fine-tune or readout fixed the readout data and clarified the primary interpretation without changing decision rules. The unpublished protocol, amendment and project log lack independent timestamps, so this chronology is not verifiable preregistration.
Uncertainty. Within each target, 5,000 joint date resamples cover all budgets and step caps; each computes recovery ratios from mean damages. Readout constraints use point estimates on all dates. Equivalence is assessed only for the five contrasts marked in Table 3; it remains unestablished between donor and random initialization at every budget and cap.

8 Cost accounting

For each cost measure, let \(C^*\) be a family’s cheapest reaching cost on the tested grid. Reuse pays off for more than \[
K^* = \frac{C_{\text{donor}}}{C^*(\text{fresh}) - C^*(\text{donor initialization})}
\] targets (Table 4). Both cheapest cells in fit-token presentations use the grid’s shortest step cap, and donor initialization uses its smallest budget; the one-eighth ratio follows from 2,048/256. The donor’s 3,686,400 presentations give \(K^* \approx 10.3\): an 11-target projection from two tested targets. Neither scalar-only fitting nor the fixed donor repair reaches the reference (Figure 3). A random start saves no presentations on the primary target; on the replication target it gives \(K^* = 18\), charged with the full donor cost despite using only the donor repair’s norm.
Unique tokens count fit tokens plus 57,344 selection positions (32 dates × 7 languages × 256). Presentations count fit tokens × optimizer steps across all four learning rates up to the cap, excluding selection forward passes. GPU seconds combine training time prorated to the cap with selection-evaluation time allocated by candidate count. For the expanded scalar search, presentations and GPU seconds also include both additional runs and evaluation of the 48 checkpoints used to choose the second start. All cells exclude base/fine-tuned readouts and the damage check before fitting.
The donor repair costs 131,072 unique tokens (73,728 fit plus selection), 3,686,400 presentations (3 learning rates × 200 steps × 6,144 tokens per minibatch), and an estimated 336 GPU seconds for training, selection and readout. The donor fine-tune is excluded because the donor model is assumed to exist.
The reference is the first fresh seed (Section 3.3); its paired interval against itself is [0, 0]. At 256 tokens and a 600-step cap, fresh fitting’s lower bounds are −1.985 pp (primary) and −1.957 pp (replication), narrowly above the −2 pp threshold. This cell sets its lowest unique-token cost. Break-even depends on that quality threshold, the grid and reference seed; sensitivity to another seed remains unevaluated.

title: Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
text:
Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
The work presented here is my attempt to understand interpretability and model editing methods more deeply. By building on recent advances and trying to find something new, I also learn what others have done before me. For me, the best way to learn is through practice.
Although these studies are written in the form of research papers, I’m not yet confident that I can call them rigorous scientific work. I’m sharing them in the hope that they may be useful to someone besides me.

AI assistance
I made extensive use of Codex with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, as well as Claude Code with Opus 5.5, throughout this work. I personally supervised the experiments and guided their direction based on the results and the questions I wanted to explore.
Most of the text was also written with AI assistance and went through several rounds of careful editing. I hope attentive readers will forgive me for that.





Selective language editing
To test selectivity, I deliberately weaken predictions in one language and measure damage to a close relative, following up on Lucius Bushnaq’s exploration of fine-tuning with parameter decomposition. Across three related-language pairs, selected subcomponent edits caused less damage to the related language than rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron edits calibrated to the same target effect on validation text. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning preserved English predictions better.

title: Repair transfer

Training the repair
The earlier fine-tune is the donor and its correction is the donor repair. The primary target is the first new fine-tuned model I repair. I repeat the comparison on a second model, the replication target. All three models are fine-tuned separately from the same base model, using the same recipe with different seeds and samples from the same distribution of European Parliament text (Europarl).
To learn a repair, I hold the fine-tuned model’s weights fixed and train an added update to match the base model’s next-token probabilities on Dutch while keeping the fine-tuned model’s predictions on German and the four other languages. I first learn the donor repair from scratch, then reuse that same repair for both targets.
Each repair adds a rank-one update, formed from an input and an output vector, to each of 24 weight matrices. I compare three ways to train the repair:

Scalar coefficients only: keep the donor’s vectors fixed and learn one scalar coefficient per matrix.
Donor initialization: start from the donor’s vectors and train both on the new fine-tune.
Fresh initialization: start with random input vectors and zero output vectors, then train both.

section: Changing the directions repairs more damage
text:
Changing the directions repairs more damage
For each target, scalar-only fitting learns 24 multipliers for the donor repair, one per weight matrix. The donor’s input and output vectors stay fixed. Each target gets its own fitted multipliers. Here recovery is the share of the fine-tune’s extra Dutch prediction loss removed: 100% restores the base model’s Dutch loss.
For each method and budget, I choose a checkpoint—a repair saved during training—on separate selection text, taking the one that recovers the most Dutch damage while passing the checks on German and the other languages. I then evaluate that repair on 92 Europarl session dates held out of both repair fitting and selection.
At the full fitting budget, scalar coefficients recover about 87% on the first target and 78% on the second. Donor initialization recovers about 98–99%. All full-budget repairs shown preserved the German effect and met the constraints on the other languages.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Edit one rank-one subcomponent
To make a targeted weight change, I select one subcomponent from Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) and adjust its contribution. VPD writes a weight matrix \(W\) as a sum of rank-one subcomponents plus a residual. The decomposition is trained so that few subcomponents are needed on any input. Each subcomponent \(A\) is the outer product of an output vector \(u_{\mathrm{out}}\) and an input vector \(v_{\mathrm{in}}\):
\[
A = u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
\]
For an input \(x\), the input vector reads out one number, \(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\). The output vector determines the direction in which that number contributes to the matrix’s output:
\[
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
\]
The edit changes a single number, the selected subcomponent’s coefficient \(c\):
\[
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
\]
Changing this coefficient changes many entries of the weight matrix. The subcomponent’s two vectors stay fixed, as do all other subcomponents and the residual. At \(c=1\) the matrix is unchanged. \(c=0\) removes the selected contribution, and \(c<0\) reverses its sign. The slider below illustrates this operation on a toy matrix.

title: Selective language editing
section: Comparing ways to change the weights
text:
Comparing ways to change the weights
I compare the VPD edit with three other ways to change the weights, all aimed at worsening target-language prediction while preserving English predictions.
Rank-one LoRA learns its own output and input vectors in the same weight matrix:
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = a_{\mathrm{out}}b_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
\]
This lets LoRA choose a different direction while keeping the update’s rank and the edited matrix fixed.
Full-matrix fine-tuning gives the learned update more freedom: it can change every entry in the model’s 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.
The neuron edit selects neurons by how much more often they activate on target text than on English text, then scales their output weights.
The VPD rule ranks subcomponents by their estimated target effect relative to their English effect. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning penalize changes to the original model’s English predictions during training.
These selection and training steps use no Dutch, Portuguese or Italian text. Those languages test whether the methods also spare a close relative that they were not explicitly trained to preserve.

text:
Matching the intended damage
To compare side effects fairly, I first make each method worsen the target language by a similar amount. Otherwise, a method might spare Dutch simply because it barely changed German.
I calibrate each edit by adjusting its strength on target-language validation text. I use two targets: an increase of 0.5 or 1 nat/token in average prediction loss (cross-entropy) relative to the original model.
I use Europarl v7, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings. After calibration, I measure the damage to both languages on separate text from 58 session dates.

  A nat is a unit of information based on natural logarithms. Loss increases are measured relative to the unedited model.
